SciWorldBench: Do Video World Models Really Understand
Scientific Experiments?

Xue Yang Peking University, Haonan Cai Peking University, Xinyu Hang Peking University11 1 Work done while visiting Nanyang Technological University, Singapore., Zhimeng Huang Peking University11 1 Work done while visiting Nanyang Technological University, Singapore., Xuanyi Liu Peking University, Chuanmin Jia Peking University, Siwei Ma Peking University     Peking University
Abstract

While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation.

1 Introduction

Text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) generation has advanced rapidly [10, 6, 18, 1, 34, 26, 28, 13, 38]. Recent models, including Seedance 2.5 [6], Kling 3.0 [18], Wan 3.0 [1], and Vidu Q3 Pro [34], generate high-resolution videos with realistic appearance and smooth motion from a first frame and a text prompt. These models are increasingly used as video world models to simulate scene evolution. In scientific experiments, changing a single condition can lead to a markedly different outcome while the rest of the setup remains unchanged. Consider an orange released into water: air in the intact peel lowers the fruit’s average density, allowing it to float, whereas a peeled orange sinks. The two experiments otherwise share the same setup. In the example shown in Fig. 1, Seedance 2.5 generates videos in which the orange floats under both conditions, although the peeled orange should sink. Generating the correct outcome under one condition therefore does not establish that the model understands how the experimental condition affects the outcome. This failure motivates our central question: do video world models really understand scientific experiments?

Existing benchmarks broaden task coverage and refine evaluation criteria [2, 11] to assess whether models can generate physically correct videos from prompts specifying scenes, events, and outcomes [3, 12]. However, generating the correct outcome does not establish that the model derived it from the given conditions through causal reasoning. A complementary line of work examines responses to controlled changes in autonomous driving and robotic manipulation [7] and simulated physical scenes [4, 20, 19]. Their focus on embodied interactions and mechanical events provides limited evidence of whether models understand condition–outcome relationships across a broader range of scientific experiments.

We introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark of 222 experiment pairs across eight categories. Each pair holds the setup fixed and varies one condition, with mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Generation prompts specify the condition but omit the outcome. Half of the pairs use an identical first frame, so the condition is specified only in text. In the other half, the condition is visible in the first frame. The two videos are generated in separate requests, and a pair passes only when both show their respective scientifically correct outcomes. A VLM uses visual evidence to check experimental prerequisites and separately assess whether each candidate outcome occurs. We score a video as correct only when all prerequisite checks pass and the judgments confirm the expected outcome while ruling out the alternative.

Across ten TI2V models, Paired Accuracy (PA) ranges from 1.4% to 24.8%, and the highest Scientific Outcome Accuracy (SOA) is 53.8%. A recurring failure is that models generate the same outcome despite the contrasting conditions: among pairs in which both videos pass the prerequisite checks and each shows exactly one outcome, the Collapse Rate (CR) is 55.7%–91.7%. Providing the correct outcome in the prompt improves generation for all six tested open-weight models, but most still tend to generate the same outcome under both conditions. The highest PA is 33.3%, and CR exceeds 50% for five of the six models. Both Cosmos models combine understanding and generation, yet their ability to infer experimental outcomes in text does not reliably carry over to video generation. Cosmos3-Super, for example, predicts both outcomes correctly in text for 63.1% of pairs but generates both correctly in only 9.0%.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark of 222 experiment pairs across eight categories for evaluating whether video world models understand scientific experiments. Each pair specifies contrasting experimental conditions and their distinct, visually verifiable outcomes.

  2. 2.

    We establish an evaluation protocol that distinguishes unmet experimental prerequisites from incorrect outcomes and assesses correctness under each condition. The VLM identifies the outcome shown in a video without receiving the condition text or the correct-outcome label, and we validate its judgments against human consensus.

  3. 3.

    We evaluated 10 mainstream TI2V models on our benchmark. Across all the models, the highest PA was 24.8%, and paired videos frequently showed the same outcome even though the two conditions required different results. These findings show that current video world models lack reliable scientific understanding in generation.

2 Related Work

Physical fidelity in video generation.

General video generation benchmarks evaluate visual quality and text–video alignment [16, 17, 24], while other benchmarks examine temporal change and compositionality [40, 9, 35]. VBench-2.0 [42] includes physics and common sense in its evaluation of intrinsic faithfulness. Benchmarks dedicated to physical fidelity assess whether generated actions and material interactions obey physical laws [2, 25, 33, 37]. Some tasks specify both the event and its outcome in the prompt, testing how accurately a model depicts the prescribed motion [3, 12, 11]. Other benchmarks evaluate physical prediction by comparing generated continuations with recordings of real experiments [27, 32] or measuring whether generated dynamics satisfy conservation laws [36]. Physically correct motion alone, however, does not establish that the model derived the outcome from the given conditions through causal reasoning. When the prompt explicitly states the outcome, the model can depict it without making that inference, leaving its understanding of the causal relationship untested.

Scientific understanding and reasoning in video generation.

Scientific reasoning has been studied both in the interpretation of recorded experiments [39, 8, 22] and in the generation of scientific phenomena [23]. VideoScience-Bench [15] evaluates whether models generate the phenomena predicted by interacting concepts in physics and chemistry. Sci-VBench [41] uses expert criteria to assess whether generated processes are scientifically and causally correct across disciplines. A correct result for one experimental setup does not establish whether the model can also generate the appropriate alternative when one condition changes.

Condition dependence of generated outcomes.

Prior work examines how changes in physical parameters affect generated motion [21] and whether a single set of physical parameters can explain the trajectories predicted under different actions from the same initial state [14]. CRONOS [4] studies physical consistency as viewpoint or appearance varies while the event type remains fixed. Other work examines how interventions alter driving and robotic manipulation outcomes [7], how initial geometry determines mechanical outcomes [20], and how changes propagate through a sequence of physical interactions [19]. These benchmarks focus primarily on embodied interactions and mechanical events, leaving open whether models understand how conditions determine outcomes across a broader range of scientific experiments. SciWorldBench examines this question across eight experimental categories by pairing two conditions of the same experiment that require mutually exclusive outcomes.

3 SciWorldBench

SciWorldBench tests whether video world models understand scientific experiments by evaluating whether they generate the scientifically correct outcome under each condition. The benchmark contains 222 pairs of experiments. Within each pair, the setup is fixed except for one condition, and the two conditions have different expected outcomes. We present the task formulation in Sec. 3.1, benchmark construction in Sec. 3.2, the evaluation protocol in Sec. 3.3, and the metrics in Sec. 3.4.

3.1 Task Formulation

We represent a pair as p=(S,cA,cB,IA,IB,oA,oB)p=(S,c_{A},c_{B},I_{A},I_{B},o_{A},o_{B}). The shared setup SS contains the scene, procedure, and camera requirements shared by the two sides. Conditions cAc_{A} and cBc_{B} distinguish the two sides and are expressed as short clauses in the prompts. A condition may specify a property, such as a material, temperature, or liquid, or an action, such as whether a bottle is squeezed. IAI_{A} and IBI_{B} denote the first frames of the two sides. oAo_{A} and oBo_{B} denote the corresponding expected outcomes, which are mutually exclusive and visually assessable from the frames.

For side k∈{A,B}k\in\{A,B\}, a TI2V model GG receives the first frame IkI_{k} and the prompt [S;ck][S;c_{k}] and generates a video vk=G⁡(Ik,[S;ck])v_{k}=G(I_{k},[S;c_{k}]). The prompt specifies the condition but omits the outcome, requiring the model to generate the result without explicit outcome guidance. The two videos are generated in separate requests. Each includes only the first frame and prompt for its own side and provides no access to the other condition. A video vkv_{k} is correct if it passes all three prerequisite checks, shows oko_{k}, and does not show the other outcome. A pair passes only when both vAv_{A} and vBv_{B} are correct.

3.2 Benchmark Construction

We use GPT-5.6-sol [29] to generate 600 candidate pairs of 8-second video experiments, following the pipeline in Fig. 1. Each candidate defines a shared experimental setup and two alternative conditions, which are combined to form a pair of video generation prompts. Each candidate also specifies the expected outcome under each condition and a brief explanation of the causal relationship between the condition and its expected outcome. We then conduct expert review to assess the candidates along three dimensions. (1) For clarity of the experimental description, reviewers check that each candidate specifies the shared setup and how the two conditions differ. (2) For scientific validity, they verify that each condition leads to its stated outcome under that setup. (3) To assess suitability for video evaluation, they check whether each outcome is observable within eight seconds and distinguishable from the alternative using only the video frames. After review and refinement, 222 pairs are retained. We then use GPT-6 Astra [30] to reformulate the video generation prompts into a structured format with four labeled fields: scene, condition, procedure, and camera requirements. The two video generation prompts in each pair differ only in the condition field, and neither explicitly specifies the expected outcome or its explanation.

In the TI2V setting, each experimental condition is associated with a first frame. We generate and edit these reference frames using Qwen-Image 2.1 [31]. The side-A frame is generated from the shared experimental setup and its corresponding condition. When the condition is visually distinguishable, the side-B frame is edited from the side-A frame while preserving the scene layout, camera viewpoint, and unrelated objects. When the condition is not visually distinguishable in a static image, as in the ice cube experiments with water and alcohol (Fig. 2), the same first frame is used for both sides, with the difference specified only in the generation prompts. All reference frames are initially created at 2048×20482048\times 2048 pixels and resized to match each model’s output resolution before video generation.

Finally, we organize the 222 pairs into eight categories based on the underlying physical mechanisms (Fig. 3). We also divide them into two equally sized subsets according to whether the paired videos share the same first frame: 111 same-first-frame pairs and 111 different-first-frame pairs.

3.3 Evaluation Protocol

We use doubao-seed-2-1-pro [5] at temperature 0 to evaluate the two videos in each experimental pair separately (Fig. 1). For each video, the VLM receives 49 full-resolution frames sampled uniformly over time, their timestamps, and a description of the shared experimental setup. We withhold the condition-specific text, the name of the generating model, the A/B side label, and the label identifying the expected outcome.

We use the same five questions to score both videos in a pair. We shuffle the question order for each video using a fixed seed. Three questions check whether the target’s behavior is visible, whether it remains the same object throughout the video, and whether the experimental preconditions are met. The other two questions each ask whether the frames show a particular candidate outcome. We describe each outcome in terms of observable behavior, removing condition-specific attributes and referring to the target in neutral terms. For example, we rewrite “The peeled orange sinks to the bottom” as “The round fruit sinks through the water and settles on the bottom of the tank.”

For each question, the VLM returns an answer, a brief observation, and a rationale in a fixed JSON format. Both yes and no require the indices of at least two supporting frames and the time interval they span. When the visual evidence is insufficient, the VLM answers unknown. We score a video as correct only if all three prerequisite checks pass and the VLM answers yes for the outcome expected under that condition and no for the alternative.

3.4 Metrics

We report four metrics for each model. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the set of n=222n=222 pairs. For a pair p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P}, vAv_{A} and vBv_{B} are the videos generated for its two sides. For a video vv, let g⁡(v)=1g(v)=1 if visibility, identity, and execution are all answered yes and g⁡(v)=0g(v)=0 otherwise, and let qA​(v),qB​(v)∈{yes,no,unknown}q_{A}(v),q_{B}(v)\in\{\text{yes},\text{no},\text{unknown}\} be the answers to the questions on whether vv shows oAo_{A} and oBo_{B}.

Prerequisite Pass Rate (PPR)

is the share of the 2​n2n videos that pass all three prerequisite checks:

PPR=12​n​∑p∈𝒫∑k∈{A,B}g⁡(vk).\text{PPR}=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{k\in\{A,B\}}g(v_{k}). (1)

This metric reports the proportion of videos that satisfy the prerequisites for outcome evaluation.

Scientific Outcome Accuracy (SOA)

is the share of the 2​n2n videos that are correct. For side k∈{A,B}k\in\{A,B\}, with k¯\bar{k} the other side, the video vkv_{k} is correct (sk=1s_{k}=1) when it passes the prerequisite checks, shows its own outcome, and does not show the other one:

sk={1,if g(vk)=1,qk(vk)=yes, and qk¯(vk)=no,0,otherwise.s_{k}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }g(v_{k})=1,\ q_{k}(v_{k})=\text{yes, and }q_{\bar{k}}(v_{k})=\text{no},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (2)

SOA is

SOA=12​n​∑p∈𝒫(sA+sB).\text{SOA}=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}(s_{A}+s_{B}). (3)

A video is scored as incorrect if any required answer is unknown or if both outcomes are present. SOA measures success for individual conditions, as in evaluations that score each prompt separately.

Paired Accuracy (PA)

is our main metric:

PA=1n​∑p∈𝒫sA​sB.\text{PA}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}s_{A}\,s_{B}. (4)

Evaluating the two sides independently can overestimate performance across conditions: a commonly generated outcome may be correct for only one side. PA counts a pair only when both outcomes are correct, requiring successful generation under both experimental conditions. A model that generates the same outcome under both conditions receives a pair score of 0.

Collapse Rate (CR)

quantifies how often a model generates the same outcome under both conditions. If any prerequisite check fails, ℓ⁡(v)\ell(v) is undefined. For videos that pass all three checks (g⁡(v)=1g(v)=1), we use the following rule.

ℓ⁡(v)={A,if ​qA​(v)=yes and ​qB​(v)=no,B,if ​qB​(v)=yes and ​qA​(v)=no,undefined,otherwise.\ell(v)=\begin{cases}A,&\text{if }q_{A}(v){=}\text{yes and }q_{B}(v){=}\text{no},\\ B,&\text{if }q_{B}(v){=}\text{yes and }q_{A}(v){=}\text{no},\\ \text{undefined},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (5)

A pair is decided when both videos pass the prerequisite checks and ℓ⁡(vA)\ell(v_{A}) and ℓ⁡(vB)\ell(v_{B}) are both defined, and we write 𝒟\mathcal{D} for the decided pairs. The CR is

CR=|{p∈𝒟:ℓ⁡(vA)=ℓ⁡(vB)}||𝒟|.\text{CR}=\frac{|\{p\in\mathcal{D}:\ell(v_{A})=\ell(v_{B})\}|}{|\mathcal{D}|}. (6)

PA measures whether a model generates the correct outcomes under both experimental conditions. CR characterizes a specific failure among decided pairs: both generated videos satisfy the prerequisite checks and show the same clearly identifiable outcome, so the observed outcome is unchanged across the two conditions. A lower CR indicates a smaller proportion of same-outcome failures among decided pairs. It does not necessarily imply higher PA, since the two outcomes can also be reversed.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

We evaluate ten TI2V models. Four are commercial: Seedance 2.5 [6], Kling 3.0 [18], Wan 3.0 [1], and Vidu Q3 Pro [34]. Six are open-weight: MiniMax-H3 (33B) [26], Cosmos3-Super (64B) and Cosmos3-Nano (16B) [28], LTX-2.3 (22B) [13], and Wan2.2-I2V-A14B (mixture of experts, 14B active) and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (5B) [38]. For each condition, all models use the same prompt and source image (Sec. 3.2). For each pair, we generate one video per condition in separate requests using the same random seed (42) to reduce sampling variability when comparing outcomes across conditions. We set the target video duration to 8 seconds for all ten models. To make full use of each model’s generation capabilities, we follow its official recommendations for both output resolution and frame rate.

4.2 Main Results

Across the ten TI2V models, PA ranges from 1.4% to 24.8% (Table 2). The four commercial models occupy the top four positions, with PA ranging from 12.6% to 24.8%, compared with 1.4% to 9.0% for the six open-weight models. Seedance 2.5 ranks first, followed by Kling 3.0 and Vidu Q3 Pro. The four commercial models, Cosmos3-Super, and MiniMax-H3 pass all three prerequisite checks in 88.7%–94.6% of their videos, yet their SOA ranges from only 37.8% to 53.8%. Even Seedance 2.5, which generates the scientifically correct outcome in 53.8% of individual videos, does so under both conditions in only 24.8% of all experimental pairs.

Among decided pairs, all ten models more often repeat the same outcome than generate different outcomes across conditions (Table 2). CR ranges from 55.7% for Seedance 2.5 to 91.7% for Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. When a model repeats an outcome, it is correct under one condition but fails to produce the different outcome required by the other.

4.3 Outcome Stated in the Prompt

To test whether stating the expected outcome reduces this repetition, we append the correct outcome to each condition’s original prompt and regenerate the videos with the six open-weight models. We score the new videos using the same protocol.

With the outcome given, all six models achieve higher SOA and PA, and all six show lower CR (Table 5). Averaged across models, PA rises from 5.6% to 19.5%. MiniMax-H3 shows the largest improvement. Its PA rises from 7.2% to 33.3%, the highest among the six models, and its CR falls from 84.3% to 40.2%. Wan2.2-TI2V-5B shows the smallest reduction in CR, from 91.7% to 81.1%. Even with explicit outcome guidance, five of the six models still generate the same outcome under both conditions in more than half of their decided pairs.

4.4 Predicting Experimental Outcomes in Text

We return to the original prompts, which omit the expected outcome, and compare how often Cosmos3-Super and Cosmos3-Nano predict both outcomes correctly in text with how often they depict both correctly in video. For each condition, we provide the full original generation prompt, which specifies the scene, condition, procedure, and camera requirements. We omit the first frame and ask what happens. The question is identical for both conditions of a pair. We manually assess each answer against the expected outcome for its condition. Both models predict the two outcomes correctly in text far more often than they generate them correctly in video (Table 5). Cosmos3-Super gives correct text answers for both conditions in 63.1% of pairs, compared with a video PA of 9.0%. For Cosmos3-Nano, the corresponding rates are 44.6% and 5.4%. Even when these models correctly infer both outcomes in text, they often fail to depict those outcomes in their respective videos.

4.5 Results by First-Frame Group

Table 5 compares the two first-frame groups in the original generation setting, with 111 experimental pairs in each group. When the condition is visible in the first frame, PA ranges from 2.7% to 30.6%. When the two conditions share a first frame and differ only in text, PA ranges from 0.0% to 18.9%. Nine models have lower PA in the shared-frame group, while Cosmos3-Super achieves 9.0% in both groups. All ten models have higher CR in the shared-frame group. The largest difference occurs for Seedance 2.5, whose CR is 43.8% with different first frames and 67.2% with a shared first frame. This pattern suggests that models are less responsive to a change in experimental conditions when the prompt provides the only cue to that change.

4.6 Results by Scientific Category

Each of the eight scientific categories contains 16 to 34 experimental pairs. We pool results across the ten models within each category (Table 6). Optics has the highest PA (18.1%) and the lowest CR (65.8%), while chemistry has the lowest PA (6.2%) and the highest CR (83.6%). For individual videos, SOA ranges from 30.2% in mechanics to 45.6% in optics. Even in optics, where models are most accurate on both individual videos and pairs, nearly two thirds of decided pairs show the same outcome under both conditions.

5 Discussion

Our empirical findings expose a sharp divide between recognizing what should happen and synthesizing how it unfolds. In this section, we trace this failure to two underlying bottlenecks—outcome-repetition bias stemming from generation without reasoning, and a modality disconnect between reasoning and generation.

Outcome-repetition bias stems from generation without reasoning. Because this bias is systematic, persists under explicit instruction, and occurs across independent generation requests, it reflects a shared prior rather than cross-run copying. We attribute this bias to visual associations that text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models learn from observational videos. During generation, the models rely more heavily on the association between a scene’s initial appearance and a familiar outcome than on the experimental condition specified in the prompt. As a result, they favor the same outcome in both videos of a pair even when the two conditions require different results. Current models behave more like renderers than world simulators, producing visually realistic videos that often fail to show how changing an experimental condition alters the outcome. Even when the expected outcome is explicitly stated in the prompt, they merely translate that label into surface rendering, accounting for their partial compliance without true reasoning.

The text–video gap reflects a modality disconnect. Both unified Cosmos models predict the correct outcomes for the two experimental conditions far more often in text than they depict them in video (Tabs. 5 and 4.4). This gap may partly reflect an intrinsic difference in task demands. In the text task, the model makes a low-dimensional judgment about which outcome follows from the stated experimental condition. Video generation poses a higher-dimensional reasoning problem because the model must map that same condition to a visual trajectory that captures how the scene evolves across space and time to produce the corresponding outcome. Even when the prompt supplies the correct outcome, removing the need to infer it, the best video PA among the six tested open-weight models is 33.3% (Tab. 5). In the original setting, all ten models show higher CR for pairs distinguished only by text than for pairs in which the condition difference is also visible in the first frame (Tab. 5). Together, these findings suggest that textual information sufficient to identify an outcome does not reliably guide its realization in video. Whether this difficulty arises from a mismatch between the representations used for inference and generation remains open.

6 Conclusion

We introduced SciWorldBench to test whether video world models understand scientific experiments. In each of its 222 pairs, two versions of the same experiment differ in one condition and have mutually exclusive expected outcomes. A VLM assesses each video without access to the condition text or the expected-outcome label. A pair passes only if both videos depict the scientifically correct outcomes for their respective conditions. Across ten TI2V models, paired accuracy (PA) ranges from 1.4% to 24.8%. Models often repeat the same outcome under both conditions, particularly when the first frame is shared and only the text distinguishes the two inputs. Stating the correct outcome improves generation for all six tested open-weight models, yet the highest PA is 33.3%. The two Cosmos models predict both outcomes correctly in text far more often than they depict them correctly in video. Together, these results suggest that current video world models have a limited understanding of how experimental conditions determine outcomes.

Future work could use paired training videos to help models learn how a change in one experimental condition affects the outcome. When both videos start from the same frame, the model must use the condition stated in the prompt to infer which outcome should occur. A latent or symbolic representation of that prediction could guide video synthesis and provide a reference for checking the generated result. Beyond checking whether an individual video matches that prediction and appears plausible, benchmarks should test whether each video in a controlled pair depicts the scientifically correct outcome for its condition.

Limitations.

Two limitations warrant consideration. First, our mechanistic interpretation is derived from behavioral outputs and text predictions rather than from probing internal representations; the deeper mechanisms through which video generation models produce these phenomena remain to be investigated. Second, the accuracy of our evaluation depends heavily on the VLM judge: even with a state-of-the-art model, its agreement with human annotators remains imperfect, which can introduce scoring errors.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
